nodes.label: Stale Cache Fallback Pattern
nodes.rationale: When rate limit is exceeded or upstream returns 403/429/502, serve the last cached value (even if stale beyond cache_ttl, up to stale_ttl). This trades data freshness for availability — callers get a response rather than an error when the upstream is temporarily unavailable or being throttled.

nodes.label: Slot Claim Before asyncio.sleep
nodes.rationale: RateLimiter.acquire() updates _last_fetch before releasing the lock and before awaiting asyncio.sleep. This prevents concurrent waiters from all seeing the same 'next available' time and racing to the same slot. If the subsequent fetch fails, the slot is still consumed — intentional to avoid fetch storm on repeated failures.

nodes.label: Fire-and-Forget Redis Stats Persistence
nodes.rationale: stats.record() schedules _persist() as an asyncio Task (fire-and-forget) rather than awaiting it, so the HTTP response is not delayed by Redis writes. Failures in _persist() are silently swallowed. Counter state is maintained in-process (_registry) as the primary source; Redis is a persistence layer for restart recovery.

nodes.label: Timestamped Cache Value Format
nodes.rationale: Cache values are stored as '{unix_ts}|{value}' in Redis. The TTL set on the key (stale_ttl) is much longer than the freshness window (cache_ttl). Staleness is determined by comparing the embedded timestamp to cache_ttl at read time, not by Redis expiry. This allows serving stale values long after cache_ttl without needing a separate data structure.
